The triangulated structure is obtained from a general cone-closed module-category criterion, before proving invariance of the finite hull. Abstract dg-category axioms (A), (B), (C) supply the generic triangulation theorem used after the module and sign checks. Technical input: Homotopy comparisons with admissible quotients and their cones.

title: Concrete cone comparisons and their homotopy invariance
statement: Let $\mathcal A$ be a small cochain dg category over $\mathbf Z$ (a set of objects, cochain complexes of abelian groups $\mathcal A(x,y)$ as morphism objects, and associative unital compositions $\mathcal A(y,z)\otimes\mathcal A(x,y)\to\mathcal A(x,z)$ which are chain maps, so that $\partial(gh)=(\partial g)h+(-1)^{|g|}g\partial h$ for homogeneous $g,h$), with Hom differential $\partial$. Write $Z^0\mathcal A$ for closed degree-zero maps and $H^0\mathcal A$ for their classes modulo degree-minus-one boundaries. Assume (A) a zero object and dg binary sums, whose inclusions and projections are closed degree-zero maps satisfying the biproduct identities. Assume (B) dg functors $[n]$, $n\in\mathbf Z$, with $[0]=1$, $[n+m]=[n][m]$, and composition-compatible cochain isomorphisms $\mathcal A(x,y[n])\cong\mathcal A(x,y)[n]$, where $V[n]^j=V^{j+n}$ and $d_{V[n]}=(-1)^nd_V$. A sequence $u\xrightarrow{a}v\xrightarrow{b}w$ in $Z^0\mathcal A$ is called admissible when there are graded degree-zero maps $\pi:v\to u$ and $s:w\to v$ such that $\pi a=1$, $bs=1$, $a\pi+sb=1$, $ba=0$, and $\pi s=0$; its boundary is the closed map $\delta=\pi\partial s:w\to u[1]$ under (B). A map is an admissible monomorphism if it is the first arrow of such a sequence. Assume (C) that each closed degree-zero $f:x\to y$ has an admissible sequence $y\xrightarrow{i_f}c(f)\xrightarrow{p_f}x[1]$ with boundary $f[1]$. A homotopy equivalence is a closed degree-zero map with a closed degree-zero inverse modulo boundaries. (i) For an admissible sequence $x\xrightarrow{a}y\xrightarrow{b}z$ with splitting $(\pi,s)$ and boundary $\delta$, and a cone sequence $y\xrightarrow{i_a}c(a)\xrightarrow{p_a}x[1]$ with splitting $(\rho,\sigma)$, the maps $e=b\rho:c(a)\to z$ and $t=i_as-\sigma\delta:z\to c(a)$ are closed degree-zero maps satisfying $et=1_z$ and $te-1_{c(a)}=\partial H$ for some degree-minus-one $H$. Moreover $ei_a=b$ and $[-p_a]=[\delta e]$ in $H^0\mathcal A$. Thus $(1_x,1_y,[e])$ is an isomorphism of the associated diagrams. (ii) For closed degree-zero $f_k:x_k\to y_k$ ($k=1,2$), closed degree-zero $a:x_1\to x_2$, $b:y_1\to y_2$, and degree-minus-one $h$ satisfying $\partial h=bf_1-f_2a$, there is a closed degree-zero cone map $c:c(f_1)\to c(f_2)$ such that $[ci_{f_1}]=[i_{f_2}b]$ and $[p_{f_2}c]=[a[1]p_{f_1}]$ in $H^0\mathcal A$. If $a,b$ are homotopy equivalences, then so is $c$. These assertions apply to arbitrary chosen cones satisfying (C), without assuming a triangulated structure.

proof.text: Use the dg-category definition recalled in the statement. For homogeneous maps, $\partial(vu)=(\partial v)u+(-1)^{|v|}v\partial u$. In particular, for closed degree-zero $a,b$ and degree-minus-one $h$, $b\partial h=\partial(bh)$ and $(\partial h)a=\partial(ha)$. Boundaries therefore form an ideal among closed degree-zero maps; all subsequent equalities of homotopy classes can be multiplied and added. A closed map is a homotopy equivalence exactly when its class has an inverse, by the definition in the statement.

source.place: Tag 09P6 (lemma-get-triangle), dg Leibniz calculations; Tag 09QT (lemma-analogue-third-isomorphism), passage to homotopy classes.

proof.text: For any admissible sequence $(a,b,\pi,s)$ put $D=\pi\partial s\in\mathcal A(z,x)^1$, the unshifted version of its boundary $\delta$. Differentiating $\pi a=1$ and $bs=1$ gives $(\partial\pi)a=0$ and $b\partial s=0$. Insert $a\pi+sb=1$ to obtain $\partial s=aD$ and, using $\partial(\pi s)=0$, $\partial\pi=(\partial\pi)sb=-Db$. Finally $a\partial D=\partial(aD)=\partial^2s=0$, so $\partial D=\pi a\partial D=0$. These identities require only the displayed splitting equations, not closed splittings.

For a chosen cone of $f:x\to y$, write its splitting as $(\rho,\sigma)$ and its arrows as $(i,p)$. In computations only, use (B) to suppress the source shift in $\sigma:x[1]\to c(f)$ and the target shift in $p:c(f)\to x[1]$. Denote the resulting maps by $S\in\mathcal A(x,c(f))^{-1}$ and $P\in\mathcal A(c(f),x)^1$. Composition compatibility gives $\rho i=1$, $PS=1$, $i\rho+SP=1$, $Pi=0$, $\rho S=0$. Since the boundary is $f[1]$, the identities of step 2 give $\partial S=if$, $\partial\rho=-fP$, $\partial P=0$. Here source shift identifies $\mathcal A(x[1],c(f))^r$ with $\mathcal A(x,c(f))^{r-1}$, while target shift identifies $\mathcal A(c(f),x[1])^r$ with $\mathcal A(c(f),x)^{r+1}$; the target-shift differential has the minus sign stipulated in (B). Thus these formulas keep the Koszul signs and apply to the actual chosen cone.

source.place: Tag 09P7 (lemma-cone), cone splitting identities; Tag 09QU (lemma-cone-homotopy), proof (1), degree-minus-one interpretation of the cone section.

proof.text: For (i) specialize step 3 to $f=a$ and retain $D$ from step 2. The maps in the statement are $e=b\rho$ and $t=is-SD$ in this unshifted notation. Their differentials are $\partial e=-baP=0$ and $\partial t=i\partial s-(\partial S)D+S\partial D=iaD-iaD=0$. The splitting identities also give $et=b\rho(is-SD)=bs=1_z$ and $ei=b$.

source.place: Tag 09QU (lemma-cone-homotopy), proof (1), construction and closedness of the comparison maps.

proof.text: Set $H=-S\pi\rho$, a degree-minus-one endomorphism of $c(a)$. By steps 2-3, $\partial H=-ia\pi\rho-SDb\rho-SP$. On the other hand $te-1=is b\rho-SDb\rho-i\rho-SP=-ia\pi\rho-SDb\rho-SP$, since $sb=1-a\pi$. Hence $te-1=\partial H$. Moreover $\partial(\pi\rho)=-Db\rho-P$, so $De+P=-\partial(\pi\rho)$. Under the target-shift isomorphism (B) this last equality says $[\delta e]=[-p]$: multiplication by the minus sign on the shifted differential does not change the subgroup of boundaries. Together with $ei=b$ and the homotopy inverse $t$, this proves the diagram isomorphism in (i).

source.place: Tag 09QU (lemma-cone-homotopy), proof (1), the identity $1=fe+d(\sigma\pi p)$ and the final square.

proof.text: For (ii) choose splittings $(\rho_k,\sigma_k)$ of the two chosen cones, and use $S_k,P_k$ as in step 3. Define $c=i_2b\rho_1+S_2aP_1+i_2hP_1$. Every summand has degree zero, and $\partial c=-i_2bf_1P_1+i_2f_2aP_1+i_2(bf_1-f_2a)P_1=0$. Multiplication by the splitting maps gives $ci_1=i_2b$ and $P_2c=aP_1$ strictly. Restoring the shifts gives $p_2c=a[1]p_1$ strictly, hence both required equalities of classes. This constructs the cone map for any homotopy square, including the inverse square used below.

source.place: Tag 09P7 (lemma-cone), proof, the explicit cone map and its differential.

proof.text: Here is the elementary null-product calculation needed to show that this cone map is invertible; keep the shifts on the cone arrows in this step. Let $v$ be a closed degree-zero endomorphism of any chosen cone $(i,p,\rho,\sigma)$ such that $[vi]=0$ and $[pv]=0$. Choose degree-minus-one $k,l$ with $vi=\partial k$ and $pv=\partial l$. Set $K=k\rho$, $L=\sigma l$, $v_L=v-\partial K$ and $v_R=v-\partial L$. Then $v_Li=0$ and $pv_R=0$, since $\rho i=1$, $p\sigma=1$, and $i,p$ are closed. Thus $v_Lv_R=v_L(i\rho+\sigma p)v_R=0$. The Leibniz identity gives $v^2=v^2-v_Lv_R=\partial(Kv+v_LL)$, since $v,v_L$ are closed. Consequently, if $u$ is a closed cone endomorphism with $[ui]=[i]$, $[pu]=[p]$, take $v=u-1$: its class has square zero, and $[2-u]=[1-v]$ is a two-sided inverse of $[u]=[1+v]$.

source.place: Tag 09QP (lemma-triseq), strictification and null-product computation; Tag 09QT (lemma-analogue-third-isomorphism), square-zero argument.

proof.text: Assume now that $a,b$ are homotopy equivalences and choose closed homotopy inverses $a^{\prime},b^{\prime}$. Since $[b][f_1]=[f_2][a]$, multiplication by their inverse classes gives $[b^{\prime}][f_2]=[f_1][a^{\prime}]$. The closed difference $b^{\prime}f_2-f_1a^{\prime}$ is therefore a boundary, so choose $h^{\prime}$ of degree minus one with that differential. Step 6 applied to this square gives a closed $c^{\prime}:c(f_2)\to c(f_1)$ with $[c^{\prime}i_2]=[i_1b^{\prime}]$ and $[p_1c^{\prime}]=[a^{\prime}[1]p_2]$. Hence $u=c^{\prime}c$ satisfies $[ui_1]=[i_1]$ and $[p_1u]=[p_1]$; likewise $w=cc^{\prime}$ satisfies $[wi_2]=[i_2]$ and $[p_2w]=[p_2]$. The shift is a dg functor, so it preserves the inverse equations on classes.

source.place: Tag 09QT (lemma-analogue-third-isomorphism), inverse square and the two composite endomorphisms.

proof.text: By step 7 both $[c^{\prime}c]$ and $[cc^{\prime}]$ are invertible. Thus $([c^{\prime}c])^{-1}[c^{\prime}]$ is a left inverse of $[c]$, and $[c^{\prime}]([cc^{\prime}])^{-1}$ is a right inverse. They agree: if $L[c]=1$ and $[c]R=1$ then $L=L([c]R)=(L[c])R=R$. Each class has a closed representative; its two inverse equations mean precisely that both composites differ from the identities by degree-minus-one boundaries. Therefore $c$ is a homotopy equivalence. Every construction used only the stipulated splittings, the dg Leibniz identity and (B),(C), so no triangulated-category axiom or special model of a cone has entered.

source.place: Tag 09QT (lemma-analogue-third-isomorphism), conclusion from the two composite isomorphisms.
